﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, that is, the one wrapped in his garment. Its original form is al-mutazammil, in which the taa' was assimilated into the zay. The same applies to al-muddaththir, i.e. al-mutadaththir, in which the taa' was assimilated into the dal. It is said: tazammala and tadaththara bi-thawbihi when one covers oneself with the garment.

Al-Suddi said: He meant, "O you who are sleeping, rise and pray."

The scholars [in manuscript A: "the wise"] said: This address was to the Prophet ﷺ at the beginning of the revelation, before he conveyed the message. Afterwards he was addressed as Prophet and Messenger.

﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾, that is, for prayer, ﴿except a little﴾. The night prayer was obligatory at the beginning. Then He specified its amount, saying: ﴿half of it, or lessen it a little﴾, down to a third.

﴿Or add to it﴾, over half, up to two-thirds. He gave them the choice between these stages. The Prophet ﷺ and his companions would stand according to these measures. A man did not know when a third of the night was, when half the night was, or when two-thirds was, so [the man] would stand until morning, fearing that he would not preserve the required amount. This became hard upon them until their feet swelled, so Allah had mercy on them, lightened it for them, and abrogated it by His saying: "So recite what is easy of the Qur'an. He knows that there will be among you those who are ill..." [al-Muzzammil 20]. Between the beginning of the surah and its end was a year.

[Note: the meaning of this statement is found in a number of hadiths mentioned by al-Tabari (29/126) and the author of al-Durr al-Manthur (8/312).]

Al-Imam Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Qadi informed us; Abu Nu'aym 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Hasan al-Isfara'ini informed us; Abu 'Awanah Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hafiz informed us; al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn 'Affan related to us; Yahya ibn Bashir related to us; Sa'id — that is, Ibn Abi 'Arubah — related to us; Qatadah related to us from Zurarah ibn Abi Awfa, from Sa'id ibn Hisham, who said: I went to 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and I said: "O Mother of the Believers, tell me about the character of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." She said: "Do you not recite the Qur'an?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed, the character of the Prophet of Allah ﷺ was the Qur'an." I said: "Then what about the standing (in prayer) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, O Mother of the Believers?" She said: "Do you not recite: 'O you who are wrapped up'?" I said: "Yes." She said: "Indeed Allah made standing (in prayer) obligatory at the beginning of this surah, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his companions stood for a year until their feet swelled, and Allah held back its final part for twelve months in the heaven. Muqatil and Ibn Kaysan said: This was in Makkah before the five daily prayers were prescribed, and then it was abrogated by the five prayers.

﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured recitation﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: Explain it clearly. Al-Hasan said: Recite it with clear recitation. Mujahid said: Recite it slowly and deliberately. Qatadah said: Be steady in it. And from Ibn 'Abbas also: Recite it at your own pace, three verses or four or five.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 73, verse 5:

﴿Indeed, We shall send down upon you a weighty word.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "Severe." Al-Hasan said: "Indeed a man may recite a surah quickly, but acting upon it is heavy."

Qatadah said: "By Allah, its obligations and its limits are heavy." Muqatil said: "Heavy because of the commands, prohibitions and limits it contains."

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "Heavy with the promise and the warning, and with the lawful and the unlawful." Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "Heavy upon the hypocrites."

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "A word light upon the tongue, heavy in the scale."

Al-Farra' said: "Heavy, not light; the trivial (al-safsaf) is not light, because it is the speech of our Lord." [[Ma'ani al-Qur'an: 3/197.]]

Ibn Zayd said: "By Allah, it is heavy and blessed. Just as it was heavy in this world, it will be heavy in the scales on the Day of Resurrection." [[Most of these sayings are mentioned by al-Tabari: 29/127-128, after which he said: "The most correct of these sayings is that it should be said: Allah described it as a weighty word, so it is, as He described it, heavy to carry, and heavy to act upon in accordance with its limits and obligations."]]

Abu al-Hasan al-Sarakhsi informed us, Zahir ibn Ahmad informed us, Abu Ishaq al-Hashimi informed us, Abu Mus'ab informed us, from Malik, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'A'ishah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that al-Harith ibn Hisham asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), saying: "O Messenger of Allah, how does the revelation come to you?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and this is the hardest on me; then it departs from me, and I have retained what it said. And sometimes the angel appears to me in the form of a man and speaks to me, and I retain what he says." 'A'ishah said: "I have indeed seen him when revelation came down upon him on a very cold day, and it departed from him, and his forehead was dripping with sweat." [[Reported by al-Bukhari in Bad' al-Wahy: 1/18; Muslim in al-Fada'il, chapter on the sweat of the Prophet (ﷺ) in cold weather and when revelation came to him, no. 2333, 4/1816-1817; and the author in Sharh al-Sunnah: 13/321-322.]]

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 73, verse 6:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾ means its hours, all of them, and every hour of it is a nashi'ah (rising). It is so called because it rises, that is, it appears. From this comes the saying "the cloud rose (nasha'at al-sahabah)" when it appears. So everything that happens at night and becomes apparent has risen, and so it is nashi'; the plural is nashi'ah.

Ibn Abi Mulaykah said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr about it, and they both said: "The whole night is nashi'ah." [Narrated by al-Tabari: 29/128.] Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd said: it means any hour in which one rises from the night, for he has risen (nasha'a), and in the language of the Abyssinians... [the standing up is called] nasha'a fulan, that is, he stood up. [Narrated by al-Tabari: 29/128.]

'A'ishah said: nashi'ah is standing up after sleep.

Ibn Kaysan said: it is standing up in the last part of the night.

'Ikrimah said: it is standing up in the early part of the night.

It is reported from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that he used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha', and he would say: "This is nashi'at al-layl (the rising of the night)." Al-Hasan said: every prayer after the late 'Isha' is nashi'ah from the night.

Al-Azhari said: "nashi'at al-layl" is the night vigil (qiyam al-layl); it is a verbal noun (masdar) that came on the pattern fa'ilah, like al-'afiyah in the sense of al-'afw (pardon).

﴿It is stronger in tread﴾. Ibn 'Amir [and Abu 'Amr] read wita' with a kasrah on the waw and with a long vowel (mamdudan), in the sense of muwatha'ah (conformity) and muwafaqah (agreement). It is said: "I conformed with so-and-so (wata'tu fulanan) muwata'ah and wit'an" when I agreed with him. This is because the conformity of the heart, hearing, sight and tongue at night is greater than it is during the day.

The others read wat'an, with a fathah on the waw and a sukun on the ta', meaning: it is more burdensome and heavier upon the one praying than the prayer of the day, because the night is for sleep and rest. From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, make Your tread (wat'ah) heavy upon Mudar." [A fragment of a hadith narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Da'awat, chapter on supplication against the polytheists with defeat and earthquake: 11/193-194, and by Muslim in al-Masajid, chapter on the recommendation of qunut in all prayers, no. (675) 1/466-467. The author cited it in Sharh al-Sunnah: 5/152.]

Ibn 'Abbas said: their prayer at the beginning of the night is "stronger in tread"; he means: it is more fitting that you may count what Allah has enjoined upon you of the vigil, for when a person sleeps he does not know when he will wake up. [Narrated by al-Tabari: 29/130.]

Qatadah said: it is firmer in goodness and better for recitation. [Narrated by al-Tabari: 29/129.]

Al-Farra' said: it is firmer for standing (athbat qiyaman), that is, more conducive to standing and easier for the one praying than the hours of the day, because the day was created for the people's affairs and the night for solitude, so worship in it is easier. It was also said: it is more energetic (ashaddu nashatan).

Ibn Zayd said: its heart is more free for Him than the day, because no needs present themselves at that time. [Al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an: 3/197.]

Al-Hasan said: it is stronger in tread for goodness and more protective from Satan.

﴿And more upright in speech﴾: more correct in recitation, more sound in utterance, because of the stillness of people and the quieting of voices.

Al-Kalbi said: clearer in speech (abyan qawlan) with the Qur'an.

In sum: worship at night is more energetic, more complete in sincerity, greater in blessing, and more far-reaching in reward [than worship by day].

Commentary of al-Baghawi (*Ma'alim al-Tanzil*) on surah 73, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, for you by day there is a long stretch of activity.﴾ That is: movement, turning about, coming and going, in your needs and affairs. The root of *sabh* (سَبْحًا, "stretch of activity") is rapid going, and from it comes *sibahah* (swimming) in water. It was also said: *sabhan tawilan* (سَبْحًا طَوِيلًا) means leisure and ample room for your sleep and for your handling of your needs, so pray at night.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur read *sabkhan* (سَبْخًا) with the unmarked *kha'* (خ), meaning rest and easing of the body. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to 'A'ishah, when she invoked curses upon a thief: "Do not *tusabbikhi* (تُسَبِّخِي) him with your supplication against him," [[Recorded by Abu Dawud in *al-Salat*, chapter on supplication: 2/145, and by the author in *Sharh al-Sunnah*: 5/154. Al-Arna'ut said: "Habib ibn Abi Thabit was much given to tadlis, and he narrated with 'an'anah, but the rest of its narrators are trustworthy."]] that is: do not lessen [it].

﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾ with affirmation of His oneness (tawhid, affirming that God alone is worthy of worship) and glorification of Him. ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: sincerely devote yourself to Him with sincerity. Al-Hasan said: strive (in worship). Ibn Zayd said: devote yourself to His worship. Sufyan said: rely upon Him completely in trust. It was also said: cut yourself off toward Him in worship, a complete cutting off, and this is the basic meaning of the root. It is said: "I tabattaltu al-shay'," meaning "I cut it off." "Sadaqah battah" means a charity that is cut off from its giver, with no claim left over it. And al-tabtil [[al-taqti'] [[See the earlier discussion: 3/32, note (1).]] is a form (tafil) of this root. It is said: "battaltuhu, fa-tabattal," and the meaning is: cut yourself off toward Him. That is why He said: "tabtilan." Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-tabattul is rejecting this world and all that is in it, and seeking what is with God, the Exalted.

﴿Lord of the East and the West﴾. The people of the Hijaz, Abu 'Amr and Hafs read "Rabbu" with a damma on the ba' (rafʿ, nominative), as the beginning of a sentence (mubtada'). The others read it with a kasra (jarr, genitive), as an adjective (na't) of "al-Rabb" in His words: "And mention the name of your Lord." ﴿There is no god but Him, so take Him as your trustee﴾, meaning, a guardian over your affairs, so entrust them to Him.

﴿And be patient over what they say, and part from them with gracious parting﴾. The verse of fighting abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revealed ruling) this [[See the earlier discussion: 3/32, note (1).]].

﴿And leave Me with the deniers, the people of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾. It was revealed concerning the leading chiefs of Quraysh who mocked (the Prophet). Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: it was revealed concerning those who fed (the people) at Badr, and not long passed before they were killed at Badr [[This was explained earlier in Surat al-Anfal.]].

﴿Indeed, with Us﴾, meaning with Us in the Hereafter, ﴿are shackles﴾, meaning great fetters that never come off, its singular being "nakal." Al-Kalbi said: it is the sand which, when you take some of it, what is beneath it follows you. It is said: "ahaltu al-raml, uhilluhu hayl," when you stir its base until it pours down from its top.
